newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya reform group hands agenda to presidency.
newsitem.headline: Kenya reform group hands agenda to presidency.

text.p: Leaders of an opposition-backed alliance pressing for constitutional changes in Kenya handed their agenda for talks with President Daniel arap Moi to his office on Wednesday.

The leaders were accompanied by a crowd of about 1,000 people who chanted "Moi must go home" and "We want constitutional reforms immediately". The leaders entered the president's office while the crowd waited outside.

Dissident Moslem preacher Sheikh Khalid Balala led the crowd in singing "We want constitutional reforms". He later led supporters in a march from the president's office to the nearby parliament buildings.
Members of a crowd carrying Balala shoulder-high beat up a policeman at parliament who tried to block his entry.

Davinder Lamba, co-convenor of the coalition National Convention Assembly (NCA), leading NCA official Kivutha Kibwana and opposition MPs met Fares Kuindwa, the highest-ranking civil servant in Moi's government.
NCA officials had earlier said they would not hand their agenda to Moi at State House because they sought neutral ground for reform negotiations. Moi was not at his office in the capital Nairobi.

"We were like a prodigal son. We returned but did not find our father. We hope he will be there at some point in the future," said Timothy Njoya, a Presbyterian minister whose hand was broken by police in riots on July 7.
"We confirm that we are available for dialogue because we are acutely aware the future of our country hangs on such dialogue," Kibwana told Kuindwa.

"We are glad you have presented your views which the government will examine and reply to as soon as possible," Kuindwa replied. "The government is committed to reforms provided they are not self-seeking or parochial."
The NCA leaders handed Kuindwa draft bills for reforms they want implemented before general elections.

The NCA is a coalition of parties, rights bodies, civic groups and churches that had united Kenya's squabbling parties in a rare show of unity in demanding reforms before presidential and parliamentary polls.
But that unity was sorely tested by Moi's agreeing to meet opposition parties this week and by the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party agreeing to some reforms last week.
No date has been set for this year's election but some opposition parties fear Moi wants to call it soon after bills are approved by parliament, where KANU has a majority.

Absent from the NCA delegation was Michael Kijana Wamalwa, the opposition leader. Wamalwa met Moi last week over security and reform concerns but fellow opposition MPs accused him or trying to hijack the reform initiative.
Nine people were killed across Kenya after police moved in to stop rallies called by the NCA to press for constitutional reforms. Many of the parliament members were severely beaten.
In the coastal resort of Mombasa, organisers said a rally to press for reforms would go ahead on Saturday but inter-denominational prayers on Friday had been cancelled.
Organisers said they had not sought a licence for the Saturday rally, making it illegal under existing laws.
Mombasa, Kenya's second city, is the coastal centre of its tourism industry, the main foreign exchange earner.
Following the worst political unrest in seven years, KANU, led by Moi, offered its package of reforms and a constitutional review which would end after the polls.
